covenants.name: Blackthorn
covenants.summary:
Founded by Tremere magi in 818, and until lately the master of the Tribunal: few meetings were quorate, so it could not be called to account, and it held most of the votes at those that were. In the last twenty years that has changed, and its magi are scrambling. It hosts every meeting: a great hall soars into the rock, magically lit, its walls painted with Blackthorn's glories (the Capture of the Wild Hunt among them), with a platform for the Praeco and presiding Quaesitor and a dozen guest suites round it, each with a barred guardroom, common room, kitchen, dormitory and four bedrooms. Delegations may stay a month after a meeting.

Unexpected visitors, even mundanes, are held in the entrance cave until a magus decides; reaching the common areas means crossing a magus's sanctum, which no magus of the Tribunal would risk. Its covenfolk, nearly all born there, see as well in darkness as in daylight, so the caves are unlit; guards wear mail, the public staff dark green, the general staff black, and each magus's own servants dark red with his badge, rotated so that no one sees the same faces two meetings running. Its hierarchy is believed strict and is unknown outside.
covenants.what_matters:
Covenfolk: dozens at least, born in the caves, who see in the dark
Allies: none among the established covenants, who are wary of it
Enemies: Voluntas, a feud of a century; Ashenrise in Hibernia, founded by Tagelyn's survivors
Boon: Hidden Resources (the caves, never mapped by outsiders)
Hook: Rival (Voluntas)
Hook: Hermetic Politics (its lost hold on the Tribunal)
Hook: Dark Secret (the old charges of diabolism)
covenants.secrets: The Wild Hunt is sealed in iron-bound caves near Blackthorn, where Flumen of Tremere led it in 1154; its cries went on for weeks and have stopped, and no one has seen it since.

covenants.name: Burnham
covenants.summary:
A covenant in the far north-east that keeps to itself. It has only lately begun sending anyone to meetings, and its envoys abstain from most votes. It holds its castle under a grant of immunity won from King Stephen in the civil war and confirmed by Henry II, owing nothing in return, or nothing obvious. Its magi may be careful mediocrities or have great and deep plans.

It does not welcome visitors: the Redcaps are treated well enough, but never asked to stay, uninvited magi are turned away, and a magus with urgent news might at best be heard in the bailey. The keep holds the sancta, the library and the council chamber, and only some servants may enter it. Its covenfolk do not talk to outsiders; they are well dressed and equipped, and recruited from outside the Tribunal as well as nearby.
covenants.what_matters:
Boon: Right (King Stephen's grant of immunity, confirmed by Henry II)
Boon: Seclusion (no visitors)
Hook: Dark Secret (no one knows what it is doing)

covenants.name: Cad Gadu
covenants.summary:
The domus magna of House Ex Miscellanea, where Pralix founded the Ordo Miscellanea in 815. Most magi of the House neither know nor care where it is, so it counts for little in the Tribunal, and keeps to itself. Its common buildings stand on the regio's first level: to the right of the path the guest quarters, council chamber and library, which guests may not enter and whose wards only talismans pass; to the left the servants' quarters, kitchens and great hall, with a roped-off yard for the grogs. Past them the path forks through two trilithons, the left one sanctum-marked. Children are kept on a leash until, about eleven, a parent cuts the rope: that is the coming of age, so its turb has some very young grogs.

Its council keeps a seat for Pralix, and every council opens, even before visitors, with the chairman saying, "Well, it looks like Pralix isn't coming"; most think she went into the regio's higher levels. Uninvited visitors are turned back at the jetty; a useful trade or great service may earn an invitation.

Since 1216 its Primus is Ebroin, elected when Immanola, who sat twelve years gazing into a pool, was declared in Final Twilight; he has restored the Council of Four. The covenfolk dreaded the day one of the other magi would take over from her. Gwydyon, a large man in his fifties gone to fat, is both librarian and autocrat, and lets the library slide; Branwen, in her twenties, is the only one acting against the decay, building up its resources and defences and hoping, without the authority, to recruit magi who will drag it out of its slump. She is a good liar.
covenants.what_matters:
Boon: Regio (Major) (an island regio whose top level has Magic 8)
Boon: Difficult Access (one jetty, and mist off the path)
Hook: House Covenant (House Ex Miscellanea)
Hook: Seat of Power (the Primus and the Robes of Dusty Dawn)
Hook: Alienable Land (Gwrhyr's kindred will claim the island when he dies)
Hook: Crumbling (a decaying covenant)
covenants.secrets: The Robes of Dusty Dawn, the Columbae's gift to Pralix and the sign of the Primacy, lie mostly crumpled on the floor or over a chair: Ebroin finds them stifling. He is an orbus, and may still be loyal to the Primus of his former House (Houses of Hermes: Societates p. 103).

covenants.name: Libellus
covenants.summary:
The newest covenant in the Tribunal and one of the largest, an unknown quantity in its politics. A dozen stone buildings, most thatched, inside a plain stone wall with no crenellations: each magus has one as a sanctum, and the council chamber, library and Stephen Eruditus's sanctum are tiled. It lies in the same small region as Schola Pythagoranis, around Cambridge, but the book gives no site. Visitors are welcome but cannot stay long; Stephen meets them, the others having little to do with the outside world. Its covenfolk have served magi for years, but have seen few kinds.

The free Jump Start Kit Promises, Promises tells more of it, and the pack does not use it.

covenants.name: Nigrasaxa
covenants.summary:
Two tall towers of shining black conjured rock, smooth but for their windows, joined by a low bridge for the covenfolk and a high one for the magi; only the first has a door. The public tower holds the guest rooms, largely unfurnished, and at its top the council chamber, where visitors meet the magi; the second holds the barracks and sancta, and visitors may not cross. It lies in the same small region as Schola Pythagoranis, but the book gives no site. Its founding was what revived the Tribunal's politics, and it is one of the larger covenants.

William of Thanet, autocrat since the founding, is very good at his work but ageing, with no clear successor. The turb's captain, Eleanor Sworder, has led it five years and means to be a knight; an ugly scar on her left cheek breeds rumours.

The free mini-saga Nigrasaxa tells more of it, and the pack does not use it.

covenants.name: Schola Pythagoranis
covenants.summary:
A Jerbiton covenant scattered through Cambridge, whose university it largely made: its magi drew scholars there when Oxford's dispersed in 1209 and kept them after 1215. Its magi are scholars first and magi second, and stay out of the Tribunal's politics; scholars among the covenfolk are the magi's peers in its administration. It admits only magi and apprentices with the Gentle Gift, who can live among mundanes. Archmage Milo of Bonisagus lived here while preparing his contest, and left for Durenmar after winning.

Visitors are lodged at its expense in the town's inns, those with a normal or Blatant Gift encouraged to be brief; the whole council meets only at the end of a season. It has few grogs, who would cause more trouble than they solved in a town. Its scholars come and go with the university, but two have stayed: Amabel the Learned and Richard Rufus the Deacon.
covenants.what_matters:
Boon: Literate Covenfolk (its scholars)
Hook: Urban (Minor) (scattered through Cambridge)
Hook: Mundane Politics (Major) (deep in mundane affairs, perhaps beyond the Code)
Hook: Contested Resource (vis, against Libellus and Nigrasaxa)

covenants.name: Semitae
covenants.summary:
The wandering covenant: about six wagons, three of them large and of iron so that they can hold laboratories, enchanted to be lighter and to firm the ground under them, drawn by six horses each, the wooden ones by four. It camps each night with guards, keeps away from towns and other covenants, and has never stayed anywhere longer than four nights, following a route Gerfallon maps that no one else can follow: it once circled London for two years at fifteen miles. The Redcaps fix the next meeting place each visit; the only ways to find it are to ride with one or to arrange a meeting. It may be almost as old as the Tribunal; its first sure record is 1151.

Travellers may ride along under its guards, and visitors bring their own food and shelter. It breeds horses unafraid of magi, traded for books or vis, a line no one else can make breed true. Its magi work by night and sleep by day in the moving wagons, except when studying books. Its covenfolk are vagrants who join for a while, wholly loyal while they stay, perhaps by magic that Gerfallon lifts when they go, and leave on good terms.
covenants.what_matters:
Hook: Constantly Mobile (a train of wagons)
Hook: Itinerants (its vagrant covenfolk)

covenants.name: Ungulus
covenants.summary:
The classic winter covenant, living on past glories and full of mad magi. Founded by House Flambeau in 984, it was for two centuries home to a great line of Verditius magi, until a dragon killed the last young one, Parsirus, and the old master died alone. Most of the Tribunal expects it to fall soon, and its treasures to bring on a feeding frenzy. William Fireheart of Flambeau, its most infamous member, made much trouble in northern France, was fined in Normandy in 1194, and lost a Wizard's War to a magus of Fudarus this year, ending its Flambeau line.

Inside it is packed with wealth, magical and mundane: guests are kept to rooms of gilded furniture, rich tapestries and magical light and heat, with more devices in each guest bedroom than most covenants own. The magi may take days to answer a guest, and those who wander meet the magical defences. Its servants keep countless rituals before doors and stairs, some disarming locks and traps, some invented, and no one dares find out which. Much of the work is done by magical constructs, brooms, knives, pans and warning bells, and by invisible bound spirits who obey anyone in the covenant; no one alive admits to knowing who bound them, and the Quaesitores found no diabolism. Its human covenfolk, all born there, are a little strange.
covenants.what_matters:
Enchantments: more devices than any other covenant of the Tribunal
Boon: Wealth (Major) (the Verditius line's treasures)
Boon: Inhuman Residents (constructs and bound spirits)
Hook: Distorted Covenfolk (inbred in a strong aura)
Hook: Monster (Major) (the dragon that killed Parsirus)
Hook: Rival (Voluntas, encroaching on its lands)

covenants.name: Voluntas
covenants.summary:
One of the most vigorous covenants of the Tribunal and the heart of the opposition to Blackthorn, nearly since its founding by Norman magi in 1083; its long summer may be sliding into autumn now that Blackthorn's hold is broken. A large stone manor house of three wings closed by a wall with a cart gate, its rear corners held by two square towers for the sancta; the council chamber and library are in the back wing. The village of Wilton, a quarter hour's walk off, is part of it.

Every magus swears on joining not to let the Tribunal suffer tyrannical rule, once plainly aimed at Blackthorn; the Quaesitores have reminded its magi that the Oath forbids meddling in the Tribunal's mundane affairs. Its library is one of the best in the Tribunal and the best open to others: study is traded for texts or vis, generously, as a way of making friends, but never to Blackthorn, and copying costs a book as good as the one copied. It runs its lands as a manor, and its neighbours think it one: Ethelwald, seneschal and autocrat, plays the lord and has avoided knighthood to avoid service; his son Edward is set on being a knight, and the magi doubt he will make a seneschal.

Founded by Normans, it is hostile to Horsingas, a Saxon covenant of the Loch Leglean Tribunal, a grudge from the Conquest that has not come to blows for decades.
covenants.what_matters:
Boon: Exceptional Book (its library, lent by negotiation)
Boon: Strong Community (Wilton)
Hook: Rival (Blackthorn)
Hook: Hermetic Politics (its oath against tyranny in the Tribunal)

tribunals.name: The Stonehenge Tribunal
tribunals.summary:
The Order's Tribunal of England and Wales, born in 817 when Pralix's Ordo Miscellanea, founded at Cad Gadu after her war on the warlock Damhan-Allaidh, joined the Order as House Ex Miscellanea. It has never been an easy place for magi: the land is thick with royal officials, sheriffs and bishops, the Church is everywhere, and every established covenant has had to make its own accommodation with the mundane authorities, not always with the Tribunal's leave. Its history is a long list of covenants that rose and fell, twenty of them since 817. There are no covenants in the West Country, Devon and Cornwall, near the ruins of Sursum and Stellasper and the sites of Arthur.

For most of its life the Tribunal was Blackthorn's. Few meetings were quorate, so Blackthorn could not be called to account, and at those that were it held most of the votes. Covenants had little to do with one another, and disputes were settled by certamen and Wizard's War. Julia of Voluntas worked for decades to break that hold; the meeting of 1194 failed so badly that Stonehenge sent no one to the Grand Tribunal of 1195, and no one came at all in 1200. She brought Maximianus of Bonisagus, who founded Nigrasaxa, and in 1201 a second, quorate meeting was called with Voluntas, Schola Pythagoranis and Ungulus. Since then the Tribunal has met a year behind the rest of the Order, and no one covenant can rule it. It has nine active covenants now, all of good size.

The meeting. Always at Blackthorn, whose Talion of Flambeau is Praeco; Blackthorn barred Immanola, then the eldest, as biased toward her own House, and since she entered Final Twilight in 1216 Talion is the eldest in any case. Iudicium of Guernicus, also of Blackthorn, presides. Each magus is called forward in turn to give his Hermetic name and covenant and show a sigil, and the presiding Quaesitor answers "Sic est"; then the meeting is declared quorate, twelve magi from at least four covenants. Business with the world outside comes first, then the apprentices are made magi, and the meeting is formally closed, until the youngest magus present protests that there are matters between sodales and asks for a new Tribunal, which the Praeco convenes on the spot: so every meeting is legally two, and either may be challenged alone. The custom dates from the Schism War. The Quaesitores do not vote, but each tells an unGifted Redcap how to cast his sigil, and the Praeco has done the same; unGifted Redcaps do not count toward the quorum. Meetings fell in 1201, 1208 and 1215, and the next is in 1222; the book gives no season, and summer is taken here.

The Redcaps. Five unGifted Redcaps, all men, ride the Tribunal from Mercer House near Coventry, whose Hermes Portal reaches Harco. Each covenant is visited every other month, two days after the full moon, for three days: Blackthorn, Semitae, Schola Pythagoranis, Burnham and Ungulus one month, Cad Gadu, Libellus, Nigrasaxa and Voluntas the next. A covenant gives the visiting Redcap three purses of 28 pennies, on arrival, at noon on the second day and on leaving. A message waits for the next visit, one or two months; an urgent one costs a special journey, at least 28 pence. A Tribunal Summons must be delivered at least six months ahead, a rule kept strictly since the Tribunal called a meeting out of cycle.

Its questions now: the feud of Voluntas and Blackthorn, a century old, and whether the Tribunal splits into two blocs; the covenants' accommodations with the mundane powers, and the Code; and a shortage of vis, as the plough takes the land and the Tribunal grows.

rulings.title: Financial Matters
rulings.says: No covenant may put more than a reasonable amount of magically made silver into circulation in a year: two pounds for each resident, magus or mundane. Blackthorn, Burnham, Voluntas and others had made so much silver late last century that its value halved in twenty years; the Tribunal judged it interference with the mundanes. A move to punish those responsible failed easily. Gold, not used as coin in England, is not covered, but magi now know that making too much of a thing lowers its worth.

rulings.title: The Praeco
rulings.says: Immanola, Prima of Ex Miscellanea and then the eldest magus, was barred from the office as likely to favour her own House, at Blackthorn's urging; Talion of Blackthorn has held it since, and the Tribunal meets at Blackthorn. The other covenants dislike it, but none has acted.

rulings.title: The meeting a year late
rulings.says: The Tribunal meets a year after the rest of the Order, from the quorate meeting of 1201.

diary.title: Pralix at Cad Gadu
diary.details: After the war on Damhan-Allaidh, Pralix founds the Ordo Miscellanea at Cad Gadu in North Wales.

diary.title: The Tribunal of Stonehenge
diary.details: The Ordo Miscellanea joins the Order as House Ex Miscellanea, and the Stonehenge Tribunal is born. The Nameless Covenant of House Diedne is founded on Anglesey.

diary.title: Blackthorn founded
diary.details: Magi of House Tremere found Blackthorn in the Black Mountains of south Wales.

diary.title: Rosalba founded
diary.details: Flavia of Jerbiton founds Rosalba in the Yorkshire Dales.

diary.title: Concordia founded
diary.details: Concordia, an attempt to weld the traditions of Ex Miscellanea together, is founded in the Lake District; it falls apart from its own tensions in 823.

diary.title: Castrum Antiquum founded
diary.details: A covenant in a Roman fort on Hadrian's Wall, which lasts until 1030 or 1031 and then vanishes without trace.

diary.title: Pralix vanishes
diary.details: Pralix disappears returning from a visit to her old domus magna (Houses of Hermes: Societates).

diary.title: Rector Maris
diary.details: A covenant on the Isle of Man that lasts six months.

diary.title: Diana against William
diary.details: Diana of Tremere of Blackthorn and William of Jerbiton of Rosalba fight a Wizard's War.

diary.title: Sursum founded
diary.details: A covenant in north Cornwall, which lasts until 931: Tytalus diabolism is found there, and King Athelstan destroys it.

diary.title: Occulta
diary.details: Newly Gauntleted magi found Occulta in the East Anglian fens; it fails to find resources and collapses in 897, its magi joining other covenants.

diary.title: The London Covenant
diary.details: A covenant in London, which lasts until about 952.

diary.title: Rosalba destroyed
diary.details: Blackthorn destroys Rosalba; its ruins are lost, and their defences are still active.

diary.title: Lux Draconis
diary.details: An undistinguished covenant in the Pennines that never has much of a summer and dies in 1100, unable to recruit.

diary.title: Rector Novus
diary.details: A second covenant on the Isle of Man, destroyed within a year.

diary.title: Roma Nova
diary.details: A covenant in Kent, destroyed by House Diedne in 1008.

diary.title: Ungulus founded
diary.details: Magi of House Flambeau found Ungulus, "the Claw", in the Lake District.

diary.title: Lumen
diary.details: An early victim of the Schism War, too poor to repel a Diedne assault in 1003.

diary.title: The Nameless Covenant destroyed
diary.details: The Diedne covenant on Anglesey falls in the Schism War; its records are struck from the Code.

diary.title: Tagelyn founded
diary.details: A covenant in caves near Blackthorn, which lasts until 1062.

diary.title: Stellasper founded
diary.details: A Criamon covenant on the Isles of Scilly, destroyed in a storm in 1163.

diary.title: Cad Gadu sacked
diary.details: Gruffydd ap Llewelyn, who besieged Blackthorn from 1058 to 1062, sacks Cad Gadu; Diedne were suspected, though it is now thought coincidence. Cad Gadu is refounded in its regio's higher levels in 1065.

diary.title: Blackthorn takes Tagelyn
diary.details: Blackthorn takes Tagelyn's caves and moves into them; Tagelyn's survivors flee to Hibernia and found Ashenrise.

diary.title: Harold's Vengeance
diary.details: Founded in the East Anglian fens to drive William the Conqueror from England; it breaks the Code so blatantly that it is Marched whole and destroyed in 1068.

diary.title: Voluntas founded
diary.details: Norman magi found Voluntas in the north.

diary.title: Lux Draconis claimed
diary.details: Blackthorn claims Lux Draconis's property, the start of its enmity with Voluntas.

diary.title: Blackrose
diary.details: A covenant on the North York Moors, which lasts until 1107.

diary.title: Magnantrum founded
diary.details: A covenant in a cave under Salisbury Plain, which disintegrates in 1187.

diary.title: Natura Antiqua
diary.details: Nature magi found Natura Antiqua in the East Anglian fens; Geoffrey de Mandeville destroys it in the civil war, in 1143.

diary.title: Burnham founded
diary.details: Burnham is founded in the far north-east, with a grant of immunity from King Stephen.

diary.title: Semitae at the Tribunal
diary.details: The wandering covenant Semitae first appears at a meeting, led by Gerfallon of Criamon.

diary.title: The Wild Hunt sealed
diary.details: Flumen of Tremere of Blackthorn leads the Wild Hunt into iron-bound caves near Blackthorn and shuts it in.

diary.title: Servus Maris
diary.details: A third try at a Manx covenant, destroyed by a dragon within six months; one magus is let go home with the message, "Don't come back."

diary.title: Schola Pythagoranis founded
diary.details: Jerbiton magi found Schola Pythagoranis at Cambridge.

diary.title: Flumen's Final Twilight
diary.details: Flumen of Blackthorn passes into Final Twilight, and his filia Goliard takes his place; Magnantrum falls apart the same year.

diary.title: A void meeting
diary.details: Blackthorn hosts, Voluntas and Burnham stay away and Semitae cannot be found: the meeting is not quorate, and Stonehenge sends no one to the Grand Tribunal of 1195.

diary.title: Trutina joins Burnham
diary.details: Trutina the Quaesitor joins Burnham, and attends every meeting after.

diary.title: No one comes
diary.details: No one attends the meeting of 1200.

diary.title: The quorate meeting
diary.details: Maximianus of Bonisagus founds Nigrasaxa; with Voluntas, Schola Pythagoranis and Ungulus he calls a second meeting, quorate, at Blackthorn. The Tribunal meets a year late from now on, and the Redcaps' network is reorganised.

diary.title: The silver ruling
diary.details: The meeting rules that no covenant may circulate more than two pounds of magical silver a resident a year.

diary.title: Libellus founded
diary.details: Stephen Eruditus of Jerbiton founds Libellus with six young magi.

diary.title: Immanola's Final Twilight
diary.details: Immanola, who has sat twelve years gazing into a pool at Cad Gadu, is declared to have entered Final Twilight; House Ex Miscellanea elects Ebroin Primus (Houses of Hermes: Societates).

diary.title: William Fireheart killed
diary.details: William Fireheart of Flambeau, of Ungulus, loses a Wizard's War to a magus of Fudarus in the Normandy Tribunal, ending Ungulus's line of Flambeau magi.

tribunals.secrets:
Blackthorn has faced charges of diabolism for generations; nothing has ever been proved, and the charge may be raised to distract from another, or may be true.

Burnham's purpose is unknown to everyone outside it, and every covenant has its own theory.

neighbours.name: England
neighbours.summary: The kingdom of the boy king Henry III, at peace in 1220 after the civil war: perhaps 9,500 parishes, rich towns, great abbeys and a dense web of royal officials, sheriffs and courts, with royal authority weak while the king is a minor. Its only title of nobility is earl. Wheat-lands, royal forests and moors; tin in Devon and Cornwall under the Warden of the Stannaries, lead, iron in the Forest of Dean and coal on Tyneside. Every magus here lives near the mundane world.

neighbours.name: Wales
neighbours.summary: The principalities of Gwynedd, Powys and Deheubarth under their own laws (Hywel Dda's), with land divided among all a man's sons and blood-price for killing; most of it under Llywelyn ab Iorwerth the Great, Prince of Gwynedd, while Anglo-Norman Marcher lords hold the south and east. The Welsh Church keeps its clas churches of hereditary clergy.

neighbours.name: The Caves of Blackthorn
neighbours.summary: A warren of caves under the Black Mountains of south Wales, some natural, most dug by Blackthorn and Tagelyn over two centuries, their passages smoothed and their ceilings raised. The door, at the back of a large cave, is hidden by an illusion of rock that fools even the touch and is guarded from inside; nothing but working along the wall with an axe would find it. The book gives no aura; Magic 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: Burnham Castle
neighbours.summary: A stone motte-and-bailey castle in the far north-east, both parts ringed by a moat from a diverted river, wall and keep of seemingly mundane build; magi are sometimes seen at rituals on the keep's crenellated top. The book gives no aura; Magic 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: The Isle of Cad Gadu
neighbours.summary:
An island in a lake among the mountains of Snowdonia, edged with twenty-foot cliffs, landed on only at a guarded wooden jetty. On the mundane level are three stone cottages for visitors, built into the ruins of the first covenant, and a path of white stone edged with larger white stones that leads between the regio's levels; stray from it, and the mists may keep you for ever. The island was a camp of the Columbae, Welsh ward-makers, where Pralix fought her last battle with Damhan-Allaidh; its name, the forsaken army, honours those who died.

In Welsh law the island belongs to Gwrhyr of the Columbae, whose kindred will not let it pass to his adopted filius (Houses of Hermes: Societates p. 112).

levels.name: The covenant
levels.enter: Between the first pair of white pillars on the white stone path.
levels.notes: The two U-shaped buildings and the trilithons; the lake is still seen, though mist hides the shore. The book gives no aura; Magic 3 is inferred.

levels.name: The ridge
levels.enter: Between the second pair of pillars.
levels.notes: A ridge path between sheer drops, with caves for the sancta. Magic 5 is inferred.

levels.name: The highest level
levels.notes: Visitors tell of a tiny island in a stormy sea, or an endless meadow; there are likely several levels, some unknown to the magi. The top level has a Magic aura of 8 (Houses of Hermes: Societates p. 101).

neighbours.name: The School of Pythagoras
neighbours.summary: A large stone hall near the river at Cambridge, known in the town as the School of Pythagoras: the library and great hall of Schola Pythagoranis, where the warden lives. The other magi keep houses in the town, sanctum-marked, and the covenant has a laboratory building on the edge of a faerie forest outside town, whose aura is better than the town's Dominion; it is looking for a magic aura. Divine 3, a town (DE p. 418).

neighbours.name: The Tower of Ungulus
neighbours.summary: A single round tower many floors high on a ridge in the Lake District, its outside covered in carvings: scenes, snatches of Latin and other tongues, writing no one can read and abstract patterns, whose meaning, if any, no one has found. Its covenfolk are inbred in a strong magic aura; the book gives no number, and Magic 5 is inferred.

neighbours.name: Wilton
neighbours.summary: A village of stone houses, unusual in the area, fifteen minutes' walk from Voluntas, which serves as part of the covenant: its craftsmen live here and its inn lodges visiting magi. Its peasants, free and serf, have good houses and magical help in need, and an enchanted birthing chair keeps nearly every mother and child alive. Divine 2, a village (DE p. 418).

neighbours.name: Mercer House
neighbours.summary: A substantial house a little way outside Coventry, home of the Tribunal's unGifted Redcaps, built in a weak magic aura (Magic 1 is inferred). Its Hermes Portal reaches Harco, House Mercere's domus magna in the Roman Tribunal. Each Redcap's device returns him and his horse to its courtyard once a day, from anywhere in the Tribunal. Perceval's wife Lucy and their children live here.

neighbours.name: The Ruins of Sursum
neighbours.summary: The site in north Cornwall of Sursum (875-931), where Tytalus diabolism was found and King Athelstan destroyed the covenant.

neighbours.name: The Ruins of Stellasper
neighbours.summary: The site on the Isles of Scilly of Stellasper (1025-1163), a Criamon covenant destroyed in a storm.

neighbours.name: Castrum Antiquum
neighbours.summary: The Roman fort on Hadrian's Wall that held the covenant Castrum Antiquum (852-1030 or 1031), which vanished without trace, and its farmer magus Agricola of Tytalus with it.

neighbours.name: The Cave of Magnantrum
neighbours.summary: The cave under Salisbury Plain where Magnantrum (1111-1187) disintegrated.

neighbours.name: The Nameless Covenant
neighbours.summary: The razed site on Anglesey of the Diedne covenant (817-1011) whose name is struck from the records.

neighbours.name: Stonehenge
neighbours.summary:
The Giant's Ring, which Merlin brought from Ireland, his art making the stones light as feathers for Uther's knights, and set up again on the plain where Hengest's Saxons murdered the Britons; its stones' virtue heals the wounded who bathe in the water that washed them. One of the most magical places in Europe. A ditch and bank with an entrance in the north-east, an avenue leading down to the valley, and within, symmetrical about the avenue's line, an outer circle of thirty shaped uprights joined by lintels, a circle of sixty bluestones, a horseshoe of five trilithons, the greatest over twenty feet, a horseshoe of bluestones and a last upright at the centre. From the entrance the midwinter sun sets between the great trilithon's uprights.

The book gives no aura; Magic 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: Avebury
neighbours.summary:
A great stone circle about a thousand feet across, inside a ditch thirty feet deep and a bank fifty feet high, with nearly three hundred boulders, and the village and church of Avebury inside it. Two winding avenues of stones lead away, one to a smaller double circle. South is Silbury Hill, the tomb of King Sel on horseback with his treasure, cursed to kill robbers, and beyond it a long barrow with a stone doorway, home of faeries or demons. The tales say that walking the avenue, the circles or the barrow on the right days takes one somewhere not wholly of this world.

The book gives no aura; Magic 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: Glastonbury Tor
neighbours.summary:
The hill above Glastonbury Abbey on the Isle of Avalon, where Saint Collen went into Gwynn ab Nudd's faerie castle.

The book gives no aura; Faerie 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: Tintagel
neighbours.summary:
Very nearly an island off north Cornwall, its neck held by a ditch and mound three men could defend: Gorlois's stronghold, where Uther, disguised by Merlin, fathered Arthur, and later King Mark's seat. Only the mound and ditch remain, and the little chapel of Saint Juliot; the castle may be somewhat detached from the mundane world, and the chapel may be there to keep it from coming back.

The book gives no aura; Faerie 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: Lyonesse
neighbours.summary:
The drowned land between Land's End and the Isles of Scilly, Tristan's birthplace, once of a hundred and forty parishes and the town of Lyon at Lethoso; at the lowest tides its forests and towns show, and fishermen draw up pieces of windows. Only the first Trevelyan escaped east, riding his white horse ahead of the flood to Saint Michael's Mount. The anger of the Fair Folk is thought the cause, though no one has spoken of why for three centuries.

The book gives no aura; Faerie 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: Merlin's Well
neighbours.summary:
On Alderley Edge in Cheshire, water runs from the cliff into a stone trough under a carved inscription in a slightly old form of the local tongue, never recut, and a face said to be Merlin's. Locals say Arthur and his knights sleep under the Edge, and the spring will water their horses when they wake.

The book gives no aura; Magic 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: Bryn-Celli-Ddu
neighbours.summary:
A mound on Anglesey whose narrow passage leads to a chamber with a smooth stone pillar; on top, by a pit, a stone carved on three sides with a labyrinth, part of some ward. Llewellyn, the last Primus of House Diedne, was last seen here, and his parting curse is carved into the passage wall, sheltered from the weather. Magi avoid the site.

The book gives no aura; Magic 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: The White Horse of Uffington
neighbours.summary:
A horse cut into the chalk below an old hillfort, overlooking Dragon Hill, whose flat top grows nothing. At certain times, or rightly called, the horse rises and goes about the country, or perhaps Arcadia, a white horse of surpassing beauty that no mortal can master but that might carry someone for gifts or respect.

The book gives no aura; Magic 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: Wayland's Smithy
neighbours.summary:
A mile from the White Horse, home of an invisible smith: leave a horse and a penny on a certain stone, and by morning it is shod and the penny gone. Wayland is said to be able to shoe the White Horse itself, making it calm, and to have forged arms for heroes of old, for more than a penny.

The book gives no aura; Faerie 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: Grime's Graves
neighbours.summary:
A dozen great pits on a chalk hill in Norfolk, each thirty feet across and deep, with small tunnels running from their bottoms; stone blades lie near their tops. Those who go near at night tend to vanish, strange lights are seen, and most locals think faerie folk live there; no one dares look by night.

The book gives no aura; Faerie 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: Long Meg and Her Daughters
neighbours.summary:
A circle of about seventy squat stones in the Lake District, with Long Meg, a carved sandstone pillar twice a man's height, outside its entrance. The stones cannot be counted, any answer from 65 to 75 coming up; harming them turns nature against the vandal, and chipped, Long Meg bleeds. They are thought a witch and her daughters turned to stone, by choice or curse, the tales do not say.

The book gives no aura; Magic 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: The Rollright Stones
neighbours.summary:
A circle of twenty-five stones on an Oxfordshire ridge, and the King Stone outside it, the most magical of them: chips of it ward off demons. They are a petrified army and its king, who go down to drink at a spring every New Year's Day, watched by the witch who cursed them, now an elder tree.

The book gives no aura; Magic 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: Belas Knap
neighbours.summary:
A barrow 180 feet long with a blocked doorway in its north face that is said to open on certain nights into a faerie palace or some magical creature's home. No one returns, though the tales describe the inside in detail.

The book gives no aura; Faerie 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: Men-an-Tol
neighbours.summary:
A holed stone in a Cornish field with two pillars behind it. The sick are passed through the hole, three times for a child, nine for an adult, to be healed; a gift laid on top moves to answer a question.

The book gives no aura; Magic 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: Roughting Linn
neighbours.summary: A rock face in Northumberland carved with more than sixty cups and rings: maps, or faerie memorials. Some magi think Gerfallon of Semitae carved them; he won't say.

neighbours.name: Carles
neighbours.summary:
A circle of forty-two stones inside a bank, three barrows within; in the east a rectangle of stones, the Porter's Lodge, where on certain nights a house stands and its porter guards the way to other places.

The book gives no aura; Faerie 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: The Black Horse of Busha
neighbours.summary:
An outcrop of black shale high in the Howgill Fells; after storms, those who know where to look see a proud black stallion, returning, locals say, from travelling the world under the storm's cover, about purposes they won't name and don't trust.

The book gives no aura; Magic 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: The Druids' Circle
neighbours.summary:
Stones on a raised bank on a moor over the Irish Sea, seen for miles. They move nearer to anyone who swears an oath inside, as if to listen, and the tales warn against breaking such oaths; darker ones tell of druids' human sacrifices.

The book gives no aura; Magic 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: The Long Man of Wilmington
neighbours.summary: A figure 240 feet tall cut into a Sussex hillside, invisible from many angles, holding two staves like a door's posts. One tale makes him Saint Paul, gaining a face as the land grows pious and fading with its wickedness; another the keeper of the gates of dawn, who will open them to the right petition.

neighbours.name: Wookey Hole
neighbours.summary: A deep, half-flooded cave hung with stalactites, with more caves thought to lie beyond the water; something lives in it, though the tales disagree what.

neighbours.name: The Cerne Giant
neighbours.summary:
A blatantly phallic giant cut into a Dorset hillside near an abbey whose monks have never defaced it. Barren women who sleep on it can conceive. He is said to be a giant who terrorised the land, pinned down asleep and slain, leaving only his outline.

The book gives no aura; Magic 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: Maiden Castle
neighbours.summary:
Great earthworks round a hill south of Dorchester, entered by twisting passages; deserted, but a faerie stronghold where those who come on the right night may meet the fay.

The book gives no aura; Faerie 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: Down Tor
neighbours.summary:
A stone circle round a barrow on Dartmoor, with a row of nearly two hundred stones running east. The circle binds a powerful ghost, which the right rites can call along the row, weakened enough to do the summoner no harm.

The book gives no aura; Magic 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: Trethevy Quoit
neighbours.summary:
Standing stones fifteen feet high under a holed capstone, one with a doorway cut in its corner: the home of a powerful faerie who does not like to be disturbed.

The book gives no aura; Faerie 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: The Merry Maidens
neighbours.summary: Nineteen levelled boulders at Land's End, with the two great Pipers to the north-east: girls who danced on a Sunday to demons' piping, turned to stone by God's wrath, and the demons with them as they fled.

neighbours.name: Offa's Dyke
neighbours.summary:
The great dyke on the Welsh border, built with the help of Huarwar, a Welsh faerie bribed with ten thousand cattle and a hundred more every fourteen years; neglected, he eats the dyke and the villages by it.

The book gives no aura; Faerie 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: The Shrine of Minerva
neighbours.summary:
A shrine of Minerva carved in the rock south of the river at Chester, left unharmed: a pagan site.

The book gives no aura; Magic 3 is inferred.

neighbours.name: Henry III of England
neighbours.summary:
Born 1 October 1207 and king since 18 October 1216, aged twelve: too young to rule, so power lies with the triumvirate of the legate Pandulf, Peter des Roches and Hubert de Burgh. He may claim his majority in as few as three years, and men jockey for his favour. Des Roches, his guardian, has made him pious, devoted to Saint Edward the Confessor, respectful of his father's memory and sure that a king's will is law, and given him a love of hunting and luxury. A handsome boy, always kingly dressed and guarded, rarely without one of the triumvirs.

Royal authority is weak: sheriffs and castellans hold that they cannot be removed until he comes of age and keep the shires' revenue; nobles keep royal manors given them by John or taken in the war; the treaty with Louis owes 10,000 marks and the return of lands nobody will give back; and his strongest officers, the earls of Chester, Salisbury and Derby and Falkes de Bréauté, obey only what suits them. The Church is wholly on his side. Abroad, Llywelyn acknowledges him and ignores him, Alexander II of Scots wants the northern counties Louis promised him, the justiciar of Ireland will not come to account, and the truce in Poitou is about to run out; his mother, Queen Isabella, countess of Angoulême and wife of Hugh de Lusignan, threatens to withdraw her support.

Sheriffs in 1220 (p. 107): Bedfordshire, Buckinghamshire, Cambridgeshire, Huntingdonshire, Northamptonshire, Oxfordshire and Rutland, Falkes de Bréauté; Berkshire, Richard fitz Regis; Cheshire and County Durham, palatinates of the earl of Chester and the bishop of Durham; Cornwall, Henry fitz Count; Cumberland and Westmoreland, Robert de Vieuxpont; Derbyshire and Nottinghamshire, Philip Mark; Devon, Robert de Courtenay; Dorset and Somerset, Peter de Maulay; Essex and Hertfordshire, Aimery de St. Amand; Gloucestershire, Ralph Musard; Hampshire, Peter des Roches; Herefordshire, Walter de Lacy; Kent, Norfolk and Suffolk, Hubert de Burgh; Lancashire, Shropshire and Staffordshire, Ranulf earl of Chester; Leicestershire and Warwickshire, William de Cantilupe; Lincolnshire (contested by Nicola de Hay) and Wiltshire, William Longespee earl of Salisbury; Middlesex, none, governed by the court; Northumberland, Philip of Oldcoates; Surrey, William de Warenne; Sussex, Matthew fitz Herbert; Worcestershire, William de Beauchamp; Yorkshire, Geoffrey de Neville.

The royal court: the King's Bench sits at Westminster under its senior justice Martin of Pattishall, and the eyre goes round the shires since 1218; the justices in 1220 include John of Guestling, Ralf Hareng, Thomas of Heydon, Robert of Lexington and Stephen of Segrave. The Exchequer, under the treasurer Eustace de Faukenberg, sits at Michaelmas and in March; the Chancery is headed by the chancellor Richard de Marsh, but there is no Great Seal while the king is a minor, and the vice-chancellor Ralph de Neville does its work.

neighbours.name: Hubert de Burgh
neighbours.summary: Justiciar since 1215, who runs the kingdom's finance, justice and patronage and is fast becoming its real power: nephew of Henry II's steward, keeper of Arthur of Brittany (whom, rumour says, he refused John's order to kill), defender of Chinon and of Dover against Louis, and victor over Eustace the Monk's fleet off Sandwich, which ended the war. Very loyal to the king, but building wealth of his own; he remembers John. Rival of the earl of Chester.

neighbours.name: Llywelyn ab Iorwerth, Prince of Gwynedd
neighbours.summary: Llywelyn the Great, Prince of Gwynedd since 1194, married to Joan, John's daughter, who swore fealty in 1218. In the war he took south Wales, but for the Marshal lands in the far south-west and south-east, and now disposes of the principality as he wishes, at constant low war with the Marcher barons and refusing royal judgement. The Prince of Gwynedd has set a court date to examine Gwrhyr of Cad Gadu, the island's seemingly immortal owner.

neighbours.name: Alexander II, King of Scots
neighbours.summary: Fought on Louis's side in the war, and presses for the treaties of 1209 and 1212 to be reconsidered; Louis promised him the three northern counties, and he may try to take them. He holds the English earldoms of Cambridge, Northampton and Huntingdon through his cousin John, his vassal, and Fotheringhay castle, which William Marshal the Younger will not give up to him.

neighbours.name: Ranulf de Blundeville, Earl of Chester
neighbours.summary: Earl since 1180 and palatine, holding Cheshire with the king's own authority; absent on Crusade (at Damietta in 1219) and returning; sheriff of Lancashire, Shropshire and Staffordshire even in his absence. A rival of Hubert de Burgh.

neighbours.name: William de Albini, Earl of Arundel
neighbours.summary: Absent on Crusade.

neighbours.name: William de Beauchamp of Bedford
neighbours.summary: A great baron, sheriff of Worcestershire.

neighbours.name: Henry de Beaumont, Earl of Warwick
neighbours.summary: One of the great nobles.

neighbours.name: Roger Bigod, Earl of Norfolk
neighbours.summary: One of the great nobles.

neighbours.name: Humphrey de Bohun, Earl of Hereford
neighbours.summary: One of the great nobles, and a Marcher lord.

neighbours.name: Gilbert de Clare, Earl of Hertford and Gloucester
neighbours.summary: One of the great nobles.

neighbours.name: Henry de Coleville of Bytham
neighbours.summary: One of the great nobles.

neighbours.name: William de Ferrers, Earl of Derby
neighbours.summary: Absent on Crusade, and one of the strong royal officers who obey the government only when it suits them.

neighbours.name: William de Fors, Count of Aumale
neighbours.summary: His county is in Normandy, seized by Philip of France, so he keeps the title without the land. He holds the royal castle of Rockingham against the government's demands.

neighbours.name: Walter de Lacy of Ewias Lacy and Meath
neighbours.summary: A great baron of England and Ireland, sheriff of Herefordshire.

neighbours.name: William Longespee, Earl of Salisbury
neighbours.summary: A bastard of Henry II, sheriff of Wiltshire and of Lincolnshire, which Nicola de Hay contests: he seized Lincoln castle in 1219, she won it back with Falkes de Bréauté's help, and he tries to recover it by bribery or force.

neighbours.name: William de Mandeville, Earl of Essex
neighbours.summary: One of the great nobles.

neighbours.name: Roger de Quency, Earl of Winchester
neighbours.summary: One of the great nobles.

neighbours.name: Baldwin de Redvers, Earl of Devon
neighbours.summary: Two years old; his county is ruled for him by Falkes de Bréauté, to the fury of Robert de Courtenay, the sheriff of Devon.

neighbours.name: Robert de Vere, Earl of Oxford
neighbours.summary: One of the great nobles.

neighbours.name: Robert de Vieuxpont, Lord of Westmoreland
neighbours.summary: Lord and sheriff of Westmoreland and Cumberland.

neighbours.name: William de Warenne, Earl of Surrey
neighbours.summary: Sheriff of Surrey; Earl Warenne holds Stamford's great fair.

neighbours.name: Reginald de Braose
neighbours.summary: A Marcher lord whose main holdings are in Wales.

neighbours.name: William Marshal the Younger, Earl of Pembroke
neighbours.summary: Son of the great William Marshal (died 14 May 1219, buried in the Temple church in London). He holds Fotheringhay castle against royal orders to give it to the king of Scots, and sues Falkes de Bréauté for four manors he says were granted only at his pleasure.

neighbours.name: John of Monmouth
neighbours.summary: A Marcher lord whose main holdings are in Wales.

neighbours.name: Hugh de Mortimer of Wigmore
neighbours.summary: A Marcher lord whose main holdings are in Wales.

neighbours.name: Nicola de Hay
neighbours.summary: Hereditary constable of Lincoln castle and, arguably, rightful sheriff of Lincolnshire, in her early sixties, in dispute with the earl of Salisbury over both; Falkes de Bréauté is her ally.

neighbours.name: Falkes de Bréauté
neighbours.summary: Son of an unmarried Norman peasant and perhaps the most powerful man in England, "more a king than the king": a brave, skilled and ruthless soldier who served John loyally, sheriff of seven counties in the middle of the country, married to Margaret, widow of the earl of Albemarle and daughter of the earl of Devon, holding a dozen castles, and guardian since 1217 of the young earl of Devon. He refuses to give up any charge until the king is of age. The Church hates him: he rode into St Albans, killed a fleeing monk and took a hundred pounds from the abbot, then, after a dream, was beaten before the monks and begged forgiveness, and kept the money.

neighbours.name: The Archbishop of Canterbury
neighbours.summary: Stephen Langton, born about 1165, archbishop since 1207: he cured a demoniac on the road to Rome, leads the inquiry into Hugh of Lincoln's sainthood, crowned Henry III again in May 1220, and wants the legate's authority ended. His see, worth over £2000 a year, is quarrelling with York over the archbishop's cross. Christ Church, the cathedral priory, is finishing Becket's shrine.

neighbours.name: The Archbishop of York
neighbours.summary: Walter de Grey, elected 1215, at odds with Langton over the right to carry his cross.

neighbours.name: The Bishop of Durham
neighbours.summary: Richard Marsh, bishop since 1217 and the king's chancellor, palatine lord of County Durham with the king's own authority, quarrelling with his monks and rumoured to worship the Devil. Saint Cuthbert's shrine is one of the four great pilgrimages; the see is worth over £2000.

neighbours.name: The Bishop of Winchester
neighbours.summary: Peter des Roches, born 1168, bishop since 1205, of Tours: John's loyal servant, guardian and tutor of the king, one of the triumvirate and sheriff of Hampshire, the richest see in England (over £3500 a year). Warrior, patron of scholars, scornful of Magna Carta, he led troops at Lincoln; unpopular, and lately pushed aside by his fellow triumvirs.

neighbours.name: The Bishop of Bath and Wells
neighbours.summary: Jocelyn of Wells, brother of Hugh of Lincoln.

neighbours.name: The Bishop of Chichester
neighbours.summary: A bishop of 1220.

neighbours.name: The Bishop of Coventry and Lichfield
neighbours.summary: A bishop of 1220.

neighbours.name: The Bishop of Ely
neighbours.summary: John de Fountains, once abbot of Fountains. Saint Etheldreda's shrine is one of the four great pilgrimages; the see is worth over £2000.

neighbours.name: The Bishop of Exeter
neighbours.summary: A bishop of 1220.

neighbours.name: The Bishop of Hereford
neighbours.summary: Hugh Foliot, bishop since 1219, whose official is Master Robert Grosseteste.

neighbours.name: The Bishop of Lincoln
neighbours.summary: Hugh of Wells, brother of Jocelyn of Bath. His minster has been rebuilt since 1192 by Saint Hugh, now considered for canonisation.

neighbours.name: The Bishop of London
neighbours.summary: His cathedral is St Paul's.

neighbours.name: The Bishop of Norwich
neighbours.summary: Pandulf, the papal legate, elected in 1214 but not consecrated, which would put him under Canterbury.

neighbours.name: The Bishop of Rochester
neighbours.summary: The poorest see, about £200 a year.

neighbours.name: The Bishop of Salisbury
neighbours.summary: A bishop of 1220.

neighbours.name: The Bishop of Worcester
neighbours.summary: A bishop of 1220.

neighbours.name: The Bishop of Carlisle
neighbours.summary: A bishop of 1220.

neighbours.name: The Bishop of St Asaph
neighbours.summary: A Welsh bishop of 1220.

neighbours.name: The Bishop of Bangor
neighbours.summary: A Welsh bishop of 1220.

neighbours.name: The Bishop of St David's
neighbours.summary: A Welsh bishop of 1220; Gerald of Wales campaigns to make the see an archbishopric.

neighbours.name: The Bishop of Llandaff
neighbours.summary: A Welsh bishop of 1220.

neighbours.name: The Papal Legate
neighbours.summary: Pandulf, an Italian of the Papal Curia, legate since 1218 and in theory the most powerful man in England, since the Pope is the king's overlord. He stood up to John over the interdict in 1211, took his surrender in 1213, and has made many of the reconciliations since the war; loyal to the throne, an able diplomat, greedy for his followers and high-handed. Peter's Pence is paid through him.

neighbours.name: Glastonbury Abbey
neighbours.summary: The oldest and richest monastery in England, on the Isle of Avalon, where Arthur's grave was found in 1190 and Joseph of Arimathea is said to have come. Saint Collen faced Gwynn ab Nudd's faerie castle on the Tor, and Saint Dunstan seized the Devil by the nose. It burned in 1184; its union with Bath, from 1195, was dissolved by Honorius III in 1219, and Abbot William of St Vigor may wear the mitre.

neighbours.name: The Abbey of Bury St Edmunds
neighbours.summary: Founded in 633, with Saint Edmund's shrine, one of the four great pilgrimages; exempt, its abbot rules the town and West Suffolk. Abbot Hugh was elected in 1215, settled at Runnymede; the spire fell in 1210.

neighbours.name: Fountains Abbey
neighbours.summary: A Cistercian abbey founded in 1132 by monks from York, about 120 monks and 400 lay brothers, under its new abbot John of Kent; its last abbot is now bishop of Ely, and it has a daughter house at Lysa in Norway.

neighbours.name: The Abbey of St Albans
neighbours.summary: A great Benedictine house whose art is famous: Walter of Colchester designs Becket's shrine. Falkes de Bréauté violated its sanctuary and kept the hundred pounds he took.

neighbours.name: Christ Church, Canterbury
neighbours.summary: The cathedral priory of Canterbury, whose shrine of Saint Thomas is nearly done for his translation: the greatest pilgrimage in England.

neighbours.name: The Abbey of St Augustine, Canterbury
neighbours.summary: A Benedictine abbey with the relics of Saint Augustine.

neighbours.name: London
neighbours.summary:
About 20,000 people under the mayor Serlo le Mercer and twenty-four aldermen; some 120 parish churches, St Paul's, the Tower and the Templars' house; five mercantile gilds and the great families, Fitz Ailwin, Fitz Alulf, Viel and Eswy. Richard Renger, alderman of Bridge ward and sheriff, is likely the next mayor.

Divine 3 over most of it (DE p. 418).

neighbours.name: Bristol
neighbours.summary:
About 5,000 people, with a mayor, a royal castle and the trade with Ireland.

Divine 3 over most of it (DE p. 418).

neighbours.name: Cambridge
neighbours.summary:
A borough since 1207, with the Midsummer Fair of the Barnwell canons (22-25 June) and Stourbridge Fair (24-31 August), St Radegund's nunnery and the hospital of St John. Its university, since 1209, has about a hundred students, at least three of them natural magicians, thanks to Schola Pythagoranis at the edge of town.

Divine 3 over most of it (DE p. 418).

neighbours.name: Canterbury
neighbours.summary:
About 6,000 people, with six aldermen and portreeves and a gild merchant; Christ Church and St Augustine's, St Gregory's priory and St John's hospital, a royal castle (the sheriff of Kent's) and a second mint.

Divine 3 over most of it (DE p. 418).

neighbours.name: Chester
neighbours.summary:
About 2,000 people in the earl's palatinate, with a mayor, St Werburgh's abbey (1092) and St John's. South of the river a shrine of Minerva is carved in the rock, left unharmed: a pagan site.

Divine 3 over most of it (DE p. 418).

neighbours.name: Durham
neighbours.summary:
Saint Cuthbert's cathedral and shrine and the castle, four boroughs and the barony of Elvet, under the palatine bishop.

Divine 3 over most of it (DE p. 418).

neighbours.name: Exeter
neighbours.summary:
A cathedral city with the mayor William Derling and eighteen churches in a single parish; the earl of Devon holds the docks, and the Exe bridge, the Gervase family's work, is unfinished.

Divine 3 over most of it (DE p. 418).

neighbours.name: Lincoln
neighbours.summary:
Its castle held by Nicola de Hay, its minster rebuilt by Saint Hugh, its mayor Peter Bridge and gild alderman John de Holm; sacked in 1217 after the battle.

Divine 3 over most of it (DE p. 418).

neighbours.name: Oxford
neighbours.summary:
A university town under the chancellor Geoffrey de Lucy, dispersed in 1209 and settled again in 1214 by Cardinal Nicholas; St Frideswide's priory, Oseney abbey and the collegiate church of St George in the castle.

Divine 3 over most of it (DE p. 418).

neighbours.name: Winchester
neighbours.summary:
About 8,000 people under the mayor Elias Westman; the royal castle and the bishop's Wolvesey, St Swithun's cathedral priory, Hyde Abbey (burned in 1141), St Mary's nunnery and St John's hospital, and the bishop's St Giles's Fair. The court often sits here.

Divine 3 over most of it (DE p. 418).

neighbours.name: York
neighbours.summary:
About 8,000 people, a borough since 1212 with a mayor and craft gilds; St Mary's Abbey under Robert of Longchamp, Holy Trinity priory, St Leonard's hospital, St Clement's nunnery and the Gilbertines of St Andrew's (1202), and the archbishop's fair (31 July-2 August). Its Jews were massacred in 1190.

Divine 3 over most of it (DE p. 418).

neighbours.name: The University of Oxford
neighbours.summary: Dispersed by the suspendium of 1209 and settled in 1214 by the legate Cardinal Nicholas, under its chancellor Geoffrey de Lucy.

neighbours.name: The University of Cambridge
neighbours.summary: Drawn to Cambridge from Oxford in 1209 by Schola Pythagoranis's magi and kept there after 1215: about a hundred students, three of them at least natural magicians.

neighbours.name: The Triumvirate
neighbours.summary: The three who rule for the boy king since William Marshal died in 1219: Pandulf the legate, who leads and consults; Peter des Roches, bishop of Winchester, the king's guardian, now pushed aside; and Hubert de Burgh the justiciar, who holds the machinery of government and grows stronger.

neighbours.name: The Jews of England
neighbours.summary: The king's Jews, under the archpresbyter Josce fil' Isaac of London: among them Rabbi Menahem of London, Rabbi Yom-Tob of Oxford and his son Moses, Rabbi Meir and Isaac of Norwich (fined 10,000 marks), Josce and Elias of Lincoln, and Chera Pinche of Winchester with her husband Isaac. Berechiah ben Natronai haNakdan of Oxford is a natural magician who may approach the Order. The Jews of York were massacred in 1190.

neighbours.name: The Island of Cad Gadu
neighbours.summary:
The mundane island of Cad Gadu belongs in Welsh law to Gwrhyr of the Columbae, who has no sons but many male kin. His kindred, who dislike him and his adopted filius Culhwch, will not let the land pass to Culhwch; when Gwrhyr dies they will claim it and evict the magi, with the law on their side. Immanola neglected it, and no one has told Ebroin, Gwrhyr sitting on his Council.

The kindred, suspicious of his great age and his name as a sorcerer, have brought him to the notice of the Prince of Gwynedd, who wants to meet this seemingly immortal Welshman. A court date is set; if Gwrhyr does not appear to be examined, the land goes to his heirs.

stages.title: The court date
stages.clues: Gwrhyr's kinsmen are seen about Snowdonia asking after him; a summons comes from the Prince's court.
stages.ignored: Gwrhyr fails to appear, and the island defaults to his heirs, who move to evict the domus magna.
stages.stopped: He appears, or the matter is settled with the kindred.

neighbours.name: Voluntas against Ungulus
neighbours.summary: Voluntas, seeing Ungulus weak, is encroaching on its lands. Ungulus is not quite dead, and may fight back; and when it falls, the Tribunal expects a feeding frenzy over its treasures.

neighbours.name: The Eastern Covenants' Vis
neighbours.summary: Schola Pythagoranis, Libellus and Nigrasaxa lie in one small region and face a shortage of vis there, whatever the Tribunal at large has; their quarrel over sources grows as Schola seeks outpost laboratories in magic auras. All three were of the old bloc against Blackthorn, so it has not come to open conflict yet. Across the Tribunal the plough is taking land where vis grew.

neighbours.name: Schola Pythagoranis and the World
neighbours.summary: Schola Pythagoranis is deep in mundane affairs, perhaps beyond the Code. Its House supports it, and the Jerbitons who speak for Voluntas and Libellus have shielded it from censure so far; it is on good terms with the town, and a covenant in the middle of a city is hard to March. How long that lasts is unclear.

neighbours.name: Nicola de Hay and the Earl of Salisbury
neighbours.summary: Nicola de Hay, constable of Lincoln castle and arguably its sheriff, disputes both with William Longespee, earl of Salisbury, who seized the castle in 1219 and lost it to her and Falkes de Bréauté. He is still sheriff and tries to win the castle back by bribery or force; she presses to win back the shrievalty.

neighbours.name: Ashenrise's Revenge
neighbours.summary: Ashenrise, in the Hibernian Tribunal, was founded by the magi of Tagelyn when Blackthorn drove them out in 1062. They have not forgotten, and Blackthorn's weakness now may be their chance.

neighbours.name: Immanola's Prophecy
neighbours.summary: Soon after she claimed the Robes of Dusty Dawn, Immanola sent word to every magus of her House that the Order was about to end, and told them to come to Stonehenge to save what they could. It seemed never to come true, and her name sank; she waited patiently, sat twelve years gazing into a pool at Cad Gadu, and was declared in Final Twilight in 1216. Her doom has not been withdrawn.

neighbours.name: Blackthorn's Diabolism
neighbours.summary: Blackthorn has faced charges of diabolism many times; nothing has been proved. The charge could be raised to distract from another covenant's trouble, or it could be true, which would shake the Tribunal.

neighbours.name: Burnham's Purpose
neighbours.summary: No one knows what Burnham is doing, it will not explain, and every covenant has its theory.

neighbours.name: The Forgotten Covenant
neighbours.summary: The magi come by a bag of old Redcap letters, many with passages cut out; one fragment left at the bottom speaks of "the two Diedne covenants". The Tribunal's list of covenants names only one, the Nameless Covenant on Anglesey.

neighbours.name: Junius's Project
neighbours.summary: Junius of Verditius, of Semitae, a powerful magus and maker of devices, spends most of his time on a project he will not speak of: people will see it, he says, when it is ready. The Tribunal and his House are curious.

neighbours.name: The harbour of Exeter
neighbours.summary: The harbour of the town of Exeter.
